title: What changes when migrating a Spring Boot / JPA application from MySQL to Oracle — dialect, JDBC driver, identifier generation (auto-increment vs sequences), and schema/type differences?

s1_definition.profdef: Migrating JPA from MySQL to Oracle touches four layers. (1) DIALECT: change `hibernate.dialect` / the auto-detected dialect from a MySQL dialect to `org.hibernate.dialect.OracleDialect`, so Hibernate generates Oracle-flavoured SQL (sequences, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` for pagination, Oracle functions). (2) JDBC DRIVER and URL: swap the MySQL Connector/J dependency and `jdbc:mysql://...` URL for the Oracle JDBC driver (`ojdbc11`) and `jdbc:oracle:thin:@//host:1521/service`. (3) IDENTIFIER GENERATION: MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT` (JPA `GenerationType.IDENTITY`) does not exist in Oracle the same way; Oracle uses SEQUENCES, so switch to `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with a `@SequenceGenerator` (Oracle 12c+ also supports identity columns, but sequences are the portable choice and enable batching). (4) SCHEMA/TYPE differences: Oracle has no native `BOOLEAN` in older versions (use `NUMBER(1)` or a converter), `VARCHAR2` instead of `VARCHAR`, `NUMBER(p,s)` for decimals, `CLOB`/`BLOB` for large data, case-sensitive quoted identifiers, Oracle treats empty string as `NULL`, and date/time types differ. You also re-run migrations with Oracle-compatible DDL.
s1_definition.analogy: Moving National Bank of India's data from one vault manufacturer (MySQL) to another (Oracle) means the lock mechanism is different (driver), the clerk must speak the new vault's dialect of filing instructions (dialect), the way new file numbers are issued changes from a built-in counter to a separate number-dispenser (sequences instead of auto-increment), and some box shapes differ — there is no true yes/no box, text boxes are a different type, and an empty box is treated as if it were missing (empty string equals null).
s1_definition.oneliner: MySQL to Oracle = swap dialect to OracleDialect, swap driver/URL to ojdbc thin, switch IDENTITY auto-increment to SEQUENCE generators, and handle type/schema differences (VARCHAR2, NUMBER, no native BOOLEAN, empty-string-is-null, quoted-identifier case sensitivity).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Migrating JPA from MySQL to Oracle touches four layers. (1) DIALECT: change `hibernate.dialect` / the auto-detected dialect from a MySQL dialect to `org.hibernate.dialect.OracleDialect`, so Hibernate generates Oracle-flavoured SQL (sequences, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` for pagination, Oracle functions). (2) JDBC DRIVER and URL: swap the MySQL Connector/J dependency and `jdbc:mysql://...` URL for the Oracle JDBC driver (`ojdbc11`) and `jdbc:oracle:thin:@//host:1521/service`. (3) IDENTIFIER GENERATION: MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT` (JPA `GenerationType.IDENTITY`) does not exist in Oracle the same way; Oracle uses SEQUENCES, so switch to `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with a `@SequenceGenerator` (Oracle 12c+ also supports identity columns, but sequences are the portable choice and enable batching). (4) SCHEMA/TYPE differences: Oracle has no native `BOOLEAN` in older versions (use `NUMBER(1)` or a converter), `VARCHAR2` instead of `VARCHAR`, `NUMBER(p,s)` for decimals, `CLOB`/`BLOB` for large data, case-sensitive quoted identifiers, Oracle treats empty string as `NULL`, and date/time types differ. You also re-run migrations with Oracle-compatible DDL.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Moving National Bank of India's data from one vault manufacturer (MySQL) to another (Oracle) means the lock mechanism is different (driver), the clerk must speak the new vault's dialect of filing instructions (dialect), the way new file numbers are issued changes from a built-in counter to a separate number-dispenser (sequences instead of auto-increment), and some box shapes differ — there is no true yes/no box, text boxes are a different type, and an empty box is treated as if it were missing (empty string equals null).

**One line to remember:** MySQL to Oracle = swap dialect to OracleDialect, swap driver/URL to ojdbc thin, switch IDENTITY auto-increment to SEQUENCE generators, and handle type/schema differences (VARCHAR2, NUMBER, no native BOOLEAN, empty-string-is-null, quoted-identifier case sensitivity).

sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through the migration layer by layer, the way I would run it for a real service.

First, the DIALECT. Hibernate generates database-specific SQL through its dialect. On MySQL it was a MySQL dialect; for Oracle I set `OracleDialect`. This one change flips how Hibernate writes pagination (`FETCH FIRST :n ROWS ONLY` or `ROWNUM` instead of MySQL's `LIMIT`), how it asks for sequence values, and which functions it emits. Spring Boot auto-detects the dialect from the URL, so in practice changing the URL and driver often flips the dialect automatically, but I set it explicitly during a migration to be certain.

```yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.OracleDialect
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:oracle:thin:@//db-host:1521/ORCLPDB1   # was jdbc:mysql://db-host:3306/bankdb
    driver-class-name: oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver       # was com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
```

Second, the DRIVER and URL. I replace the MySQL Connector/J Maven dependency with the Oracle driver (`com.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc11`) and change the JDBC URL to the Oracle thin format with host, port 1521, and the service name. Oracle licensing and the driver artifact differ, so I confirm the dependency is available in the build.

Third, IDENTIFIER GENERATION — the biggest code change. On MySQL I typically used `GenerationType.IDENTITY`, backed by `AUTO_INCREMENT`. Oracle historically had no auto-increment; it uses SEQUENCE objects. So I change the entity to `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with a `@SequenceGenerator`, and I create the sequence in the Oracle schema. As a bonus, sequences let Hibernate pre-allocate id blocks and batch inserts, which IDENTITY could not.

```java
// MySQL (before):
// @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;

// Oracle (after):
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq_gen")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "account_seq_gen", sequenceName = "account_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;
```

Fourth, SCHEMA and TYPE differences, which cause the subtle runtime surprises:
- `VARCHAR` becomes `VARCHAR2` in Oracle DDL (Hibernate's Oracle dialect handles the mapping, but hand-written DDL must change).
- Decimals use `NUMBER(p,s)` instead of MySQL's `DECIMAL(p,s)` — for money I keep `BigDecimal` fields with precision and scale so Hibernate emits `NUMBER(15,2)`.
- BOOLEAN: older Oracle has no native boolean type. A Java `boolean` maps to `NUMBER(1)`; I rely on the dialect or an `AttributeConverter` to store 1/0. (Oracle 23c adds a real boolean, but I do not assume it.)
- Large text/binary: MySQL `TEXT`/`BLOB` becomes Oracle `CLOB`/`BLOB`.
- EMPTY STRING IS NULL: Oracle treats `''` as `NULL`. Code or queries that rely on distinguishing an empty string from null (common habit on MySQL) will behave differently, so I audit `NOT NULL` columns and `= ''` comparisons.
- IDENTIFIER CASE: Oracle folds unquoted identifiers to UPPERCASE and is case-sensitive for quoted ones. I keep naming consistent and avoid quoted mixed-case names.
- Date/time: `DATE` in Oracle includes a time component; I use `TIMESTAMP` for precise timestamps and map `LocalDateTime` accordingly.

I also re-run schema migrations with Oracle-compatible DDL (a separate Flyway/Liquibase script set or database-specific migrations), and I set `ddl-auto: validate` so Hibernate verifies the entity mappings against the real Oracle schema at startup.

A senior point on process: I do a migration in stages — first make the application dialect/driver-agnostic by using JPA portable features (avoid native MySQL SQL, avoid MySQL-only functions), then switch the dialect and driver, then run the full regression and integration tests against a real Oracle instance, because dialect translation covers generated SQL but not any native queries or vendor-specific tricks the team may have slipped in.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the migration we ran at National Bank of India when a regulatory programme mandated Oracle for the core ledger.

Problem 1 — auto-increment keys did not exist in Oracle. The account and transaction tables used MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT` with `GenerationType.IDENTITY`, which Oracle does not provide in the same way. This is exactly the sequence change: we created Oracle sequences and switched the entities to `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with sequence generators, which also enabled insert batching we never had on MySQL.

Problem 2 — pagination SQL broke. Repository pagination relied on MySQL `LIMIT`, and a couple of native queries used `LIMIT` explicitly. Hibernate's generated pagination was fixed automatically by switching to the Oracle dialect (it emits `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`), but the hand-written native `LIMIT` queries had to be rewritten. This is exactly why I audit native SQL before flipping the dialect.

Problem 3 — a boolean flag and an empty-string check misbehaved. An `active` boolean flag and some code that treated an empty string as distinct from null worked on MySQL but changed behaviour on Oracle, where there is no native boolean and empty string is null. This is exactly the type/semantic difference: we mapped the boolean to `NUMBER(1)` via the dialect and audited the empty-string comparisons.

Problem 4 — money columns needed the right type. MySQL `DECIMAL(15,2)` became Oracle `NUMBER(15,2)`; keeping `BigDecimal` with precision and scale made Hibernate emit the correct type on both.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity whose key uses `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with an Oracle sequence generator, a `BigDecimal balance` with precision and scale (portable to `NUMBER(15,2)`), a boolean `active` mapped via a converter to a 1/0 number, and large `notes` mapped as a CLOB. The configuration shows the Oracle dialect, driver, and thin URL, with the previous MySQL values commented for contrast. The `AccountService`, annotated `@Transactional`, creates an account (sequence-generated id, batchable) and reads it back. A test documents the before/after for each migration layer and verifies the entity now uses SEQUENCE, not IDENTITY. The SQL script is Oracle-compatible DDL.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is opening Amit's account after the migration to Oracle.

Step 1 — connection. At startup Spring connects using the Oracle thin URL (`jdbc:oracle:thin:@//db-host:1521/ORCLPDB1`) and the Oracle driver, instead of the old MySQL URL and Connector/J. The dialect is set to OracleDialect, so Hibernate will generate Oracle SQL.

Step 2 — id generation. `open(...)` constructs an `Account` with no id. Because the key uses `GenerationType.SEQUENCE`, Hibernate runs `SELECT account_seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual` to obtain an id — this is the Oracle mechanism, replacing MySQL's auto-increment. With `allocationSize = 50`, one sequence call reserves fifty ids, and because the id is known before flush, Hibernate can batch inserts, which it could never do with the old IDENTITY strategy.

Step 3 — insert with Oracle types. On save, Hibernate issues `INSERT INTO accounts (id, holder_name, balance, active, notes, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)`. The `balance` BigDecimal maps to `NUMBER(15,2)`; the `active` boolean passes through the converter and is stored as `NUMBER(1)` value 1; the `notes` string is stored as a `CLOB`; `created_at` is a `TIMESTAMP`.

Step 4 — semantic differences handled. Because Oracle treats an empty string as NULL, any field that must distinguish empty from null was audited during migration; here `notes` is nullable so an empty input simply becomes NULL, which is the Oracle behaviour. Identifier case is consistent (unquoted, folded to uppercase by Oracle), so no quoted mixed-case surprises.

Step 5 — read back. `view(id)` loads the account. Pagination queries elsewhere now emit `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` because of the Oracle dialect, not MySQL `LIMIT`. The response includes the sequence-generated id and the Oracle-typed values, and the migration note lists the four layers that changed.

```
2026-10-24 01:00:30 INFO  AccountService - SELECT account_seq.NEXTVAL (Oracle sequence) → id block of 50
2026-10-24 01:00:30 FINE  AccountService - INSERT accounts (id, holder_name, balance NUMBER(15,2), active NUMBER(1), notes CLOB)
2026-10-24 01:00:30 INFO  AccountService - Opened account id=3 via SEQUENCE (Oracle), batching enabled
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ FOUR MIGRATION LAYERS: MySQL → Oracle ═══

  1) DIALECT
     MySQLDialect ──→ OracleDialect
     pagination: LIMIT n OFFSET m  →  OFFSET m ROWS FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
     id request: (auto-increment)  →  SELECT seq.NEXTVAL FROM dual

  2) DRIVER / URL
     com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver      →  oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver
     jdbc:mysql://host:3306/bankdb →  jdbc:oracle:thin:@//host:1521/ORCLPDB1

  3) ID GENERATION
     @GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)      →  @GeneratedValue(SEQUENCE) + @SequenceGenerator
     AUTO_INCREMENT column          →  CREATE SEQUENCE account_seq
     (bonus) no batching            →  allocationSize block → batched INSERTs

  4) SCHEMA / TYPES / SEMANTICS
     VARCHAR        → VARCHAR2
     DECIMAL(p,s)   → NUMBER(p,s)        (money: BigDecimal precision+scale)
     BOOLEAN/TINYINT→ NUMBER(1) + converter (pre-23c)
     TEXT / BLOB    → CLOB / BLOB
     ''  (empty)    → NULL               (Oracle empty-string = NULL!)
     identifiers    → UPPERCASE unless quoted (case-sensitive if quoted)
     DATETIME       → TIMESTAMP

  (Caution) Native MySQL SQL (LIMIT, functions) must be rewritten — dialect fixes only generated SQL.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Migrating a JPA application from MySQL to Oracle touches four layers. First the dialect: I change Hibernate's dialect to the Oracle dialect so it generates Oracle-flavoured SQL, which affects pagination, where MySQL's LIMIT becomes Oracle's FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, and it affects how Hibernate requests identifiers. Second the driver and URL: I swap the MySQL Connector/J dependency and the jdbc:mysql URL for the Oracle thin driver and a jdbc:oracle:thin URL on port 1521 with the service name. Third, and this is the biggest code change, identifier generation: MySQL auto-increment with GenerationType.IDENTITY does not exist in Oracle the same way, so I switch to GenerationType.SEQUENCE with a sequence generator and create the Oracle sequence, which as a bonus lets Hibernate pre-allocate id blocks and batch inserts, something IDENTITY never allowed. Fourth, schema and type differences: VARCHAR becomes VARCHAR2, DECIMAL becomes NUMBER with precision and scale for money, older Oracle has no native boolean so a Java boolean maps to NUMBER(1) through a converter, large text becomes CLOB, and crucially Oracle treats an empty string as null.

In our core ledger migration at National Bank of India, the account and transaction tables moved from auto-increment keys to Oracle sequences, which also gave us insert batching we never had on MySQL, and the money columns moved from DECIMAL to NUMBER while staying BigDecimal in Java so the mapping was correct on both. We mapped the active flag through a boolean-to-number converter and the notes field to a CLOB.

The senior point I always stress is that the dialect only fixes Hibernate's generated SQL, not any native SQL the team wrote by hand. So before flipping the dialect I audit every native query for MySQL-only constructs like LIMIT or MySQL-specific functions and rewrite them, I audit any code that relied on an empty string being distinct from null because Oracle collapses the two, and I keep identifier naming consistent because Oracle folds unquoted names to uppercase and is case-sensitive for quoted ones. I run the migration in stages with ddl-auto set to validate against a real Oracle instance and a full regression pass, because correctness across the whole application is what the migration must guarantee, not just that the generated SQL compiles.
